text: His nickname was Hellish Brueghel, given on the belief that he painted the fantastic fire and grotesque scenes now credited to his brother Jan. Pieter Brueghel the Younger made numerous copies of his father's work, plus some original compositions. Around 1,400 pictures have plausible links to him and his shop. The workshop sold at home and abroad, and so helped spread his father's imagery across Europe. He died in 1638.

Étienne Fessard learned engraving from Edme Jeaurat in Paris. The comte de Caylus took him up, and in 1756 Fessard became Engraver of the King's Library, in charge of engraving the royal collection of paintings and drawings. He cut a considerable number of plates. His effort to resume the engraving of the King's paintings got no support from the Académie royale, and produced only two plates, after Rubens and Poussin. He died in 1777, and his student Augustin de Saint-Aubin got the post.

Luca Signorelli painted a lost section of the Sistine Chapel while working in Rome, then moved back to Cortona in his early forties. He stayed there for the rest of his life but travelled to nearby cities for commissions. Giorgio Vasari, his cousin, wrote that he probably trained under Piero della Francesca. His huge frescoes of the Last Judgment in Orvieto Cathedral are counted as his masterpiece. He was noted for his draftsmanship and for foreshortening.

Torii Kiyomasu worked mainly on Kabuki billboards, advertisements and actor prints. Scholars think he was the younger brother or son of Torii Kiyonobu I, or even the same man under another art-name. In the 1710s, prints signed Kiyomasu far outnumber those signed Kiyonobu. If they were two artists, the elder may have spent more time on the official billboards. His style is said to be somewhat more graceful. He belonged to the Torii school of ukiyo-e.

Candlelight fills most of what Georges de La Tour painted, mostly religious scenes in strong light and shadow. He spent most of his working life in the Duchy of Lorraine. He took a keen look at everyday reality and a taste for simplified forms, which makes him one of Caravaggio's most original successors. People recognised him in his lifetime, and then forgot him soon after his death. The German art historian Hermann Voss rediscovered him in the early 20th century.

Choir books, pavement designs and frescoes all came from Benvenuto di Giovanni, who worked chiefly in Siena. He was first recorded as an artist in 1453 and kept working nearly to his death. His style changed drastically in the 1480s. His son Girolamo di Giovanni also became a painter, and their works have often been confused. Benvenuto left far more. Some of his works are signed and dated, some only signed, some only dated.

Salomon Koninck made many copies of Rembrandt's compositions while moving in Rembrandt's circle and the academy of Hendrick van Uylenburgh. He was born in Amsterdam, the son of a goldsmith from Antwerp, and studied under Pieter Lastman and others. His paintings have warm colours and include many philosophers or scholars. One of them, in the Louvre, was long attributed to Rembrandt. He married a daughter of Adriaen van Nieulandt. He died in Amsterdam in 1656.

Nobody knows the name of the Master of the Osservanza Triptych. Roberto Longhi saw that two triptychs once given to Sassetta were by another hand, and the name comes from one of them, in the Basilica dell'Osservanza in Siena. The painter was active in Siena between about 1430 and 1450. His work resembles Sassetta's, but his storytelling is more characteristic of Late Gothic painting. Longhi grouped other paintings with these.

Benedetto Montagna trained with his father Bartolomeo, the leading painter of Vicenza, and inherited his workshop in 1523. He made about 53 engravings, mostly between 1500 and his father's death, and was then the most prolific engraver of his generation in northern Italy. They show subjects from classical mythology, with a middle period of religious subjects. His paintings followed his father's style less successfully, and many are lost. Art historians rate his prints higher.

The Master of Frankfurt probably never visited Frankfurt. His name comes from two paintings commissioned by patrons in that city. He worked in Antwerp between about 1480 and 1520. A dated self-portrait with his wife, from 1496, shows that he was 36 then and a member of the Guild of St Luke. Often he is identified as Hendrik van Wueluwe. If so, he served as dean of the guild six times.

Cornelis de Heem was baptised in Leiden and moved with his family to Antwerp in 1636, where his father Jan Davidszoon de Heem trained him. He joined the Antwerp painters' guild in 1660. From 1667 until the late 1680s he worked in Utrecht, IJsselstein and The Hague. He painted still lifes. The family had many still-life specialists, and it is often hard to tell their works apart.

Domenico Veneziano is thought to have been born in Venice, which explains his name. As a boy he moved to Florence and became a pupil of Gentile da Fabriano. In a letter of 1438 from Perugia he begged Piero di Cosimo de' Medici to let him paint an altarpiece for the family. Between 1439 and 1441 he painted the Adoration of the Magi, a round panel. Fra Angelico and Fra Filippo Lippi were his contemporaries. Little else is known of his early life.

Sentimental watercolours of country children made Myles Birket Foster both famous and rich. They gave an idealized view of rural life in southern England. The Times called him certainly the most popular water-colour artist of our time. Early on he also painted fine landscapes, often with buildings. Late in his career he was copied and faked a lot, because he signed with a simple monogram that was easy to imitate. He worked as an illustrator and engraver too.

Portraits of the Habsburg court at Innsbruck and of rich merchants like the Fuggers were the business of Hans Maler zu Schwaz. He came from Ulm and may have trained with Bartholomäus Zeitblom. His two main patrons were Archduke Ferdinand, later Emperor, and the Fuggers. Ferdinand commissioned at least three portraits of himself and four of his wife Anna. Maler rarely varied his format, a bust with no hands shown and no eye contact with the viewer.

Herter Brothers, the New York interior design firm his father Christian co-founded, closed in 1906, and Albert Herter started Herter Looms three years later to make tapestries and textiles. Albert was born in New York City and studied at the Art Students League with James Carroll Beckwith. In Paris he studied with Jean-Paul Laurens and Fernand Cormon. He painted, illustrated, made murals and designed interiors. He lived from 1871 to 1950.

Jacek Malczewski's father Julian, a Polish patriot, introduced him as a child to romantic literature inspired by the November Uprising. He grew up in Radom under Russian occupation. His paintings mix the leading style of his time with Polish martyrdom, hopes of independence, mythology, folk tales and a love of nature. He was a central figure of the patriotic Young Poland movement. His son Rafał became a painter too. He lived from 1854 to 1929.

George III took such a fatherly interest in young John Hoppner that people spread a rumour, quite unfounded, that he was the king's son. Hoppner's mother was one of the German attendants at the royal palace. He sang as a chorister at the royal chapel and entered the Royal Academy in 1775. In 1782 he won its gold medal for historical painting with a King Lear. He mostly painted portraits of London high society and was much influenced by Reynolds.

Matisse and Albert Marquet were roommates for a time in Paris, after they met at the École des Arts Décoratifs. Marquet came from Bordeaux and moved to Paris at fifteen. He later studied under Gustave Moreau. He started out as one of the Fauves and then painted in a more impressionist way, mainly landscapes. A few portraits and, between 1910 and 1914, several female nudes also exist. He showed at the Salon des Indépendants but sold few paintings at first.

Frozen canals with skaters were what made Andreas Schelfhout famous in his own lifetime. He began as a house painter in his father's framing business and painted pictures in his spare time. After a well-received first show in The Hague, his father sent him to the stage designer Joannes Breckenheimer for training. He also studied the 17th-century landscapes of Hobbema and Ruisdael. In 1815 he started his own workshop. He became one of the most influential Dutch landscape artists of his century.

Thomas Ender had a twin brother, Johann Nepomuk, who became a history painter, and the two enrolled together at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna. Thomas started with history painting but switched to landscape. After the death of his teacher Laurenz Janscha he studied with Joseph Mössmer. Prince Metternich bought his prize-winning canvas, became his patron, and made it possible for him to join the Austrian Brazilian Expedition. There he made over 700 drawings and watercolors.

After 1630 Ferdinand Bol lived in Rembrandt's house on the Sint Antoniesbreestraat as his apprentice. He came from Dordrecht, where his father was a surgeon, and had first trained with Jacob Cuyp or Abraham Bloemaert. He started his own studio in 1641 and became a burgher of Amsterdam in 1652. A year later he married Elisabeth Dell. Little of his work survives. What does shows Rembrandt's influence in its historical subjects, portraits and self-portraits.

Jacques Reich drew portraits for Appletons' Cyclopædia of American Biography, more than 2,000 of them. He was born in Hungary in what is now Slovakia, studied art in Budapest, and came to the United States in 1873. He studied at the National Academy of Design and in Philadelphia, and spent a year in Paris with Bouguereau and Robert-Fleury, probably changing his name to Jacques then. He moved to New York in 1885. He etched portraits.

A theatrical family raised Józef Rapacki in Warsaw, and his father Wincenty was an actor, as were his brother and sister. He chose differently and joined Wojciech Gerson's drawing class at fourteen. Then he studied at the Kraków Academy of Fine Arts. In 1889 he went to Munich and studied two years with the portrait painter Conrad Fehr. His best known pictures are nostalgic landscapes of Mazovia. He also painted watercolors and made graphic designs.

Very little is known about Adriaen Coorte. He probably came from Middelburg, and worked there for much of his career. Around 1680 he became a pupil of Melchior d'Hondecoeter in Amsterdam. He signed paintings between 1683 and 1707. His still lifes are small and restrained: fruit, vegetables and shells on stone ledges against dark backgrounds. He has been described as one of the last practitioners of that intimate category.

Paul Bril spent most of his working life in Rome, painting Italianate landscapes that were influential in Italy and northern Europe. He is credited as a pioneer of the wooded landscape. He was probably born in Antwerp, though Breda is possible. His father was the painter Mathys Baertmaker, and four of his brothers also became painters. The brothers probably began their training with their father. Bril died in 1626.

Ralph Blakelock set out to be a physician like his father but dropped out of the Free Academy of the City of New York after three terms. From 1869 to 1872 he travelled alone through the American West, spending time among Native Americans. Largely self-taught, he turned his notebooks into competent landscapes and scenes of Indian life. He is known mainly for landscapes related to Tonalism.

Flower still lifes sold for high prices, and that is why Jacob Marrel studied in Utrecht with Jan Davidszoon de Heem. Before that, his family moved from Frankenthal to Frankfurt when he was a boy, and he trained with Georg Flegel. Back in Frankfurt he married Johanna Sybilla Heim, the widow of Matthäus Merian. Her daughter Maria Sibylla Merian became a famous painter of flowers and insects. She later married one of Marrel's pupils, Johann Andreas Graff.

Dominic Serres started out studying for the priesthood in Douai, left, and ended up as a merchant captain in Cuba. Britain captured him in the Caribbean in 1748 and took him to England as a prisoner. Later he became a marine painter. He co-founded the Royal Academy in 1768 and served as its librarian from 1792 until his death. He came from Auch, in Gascony.

Alberto Pasini's father died when he was two, and his mother took him to Parma. He enrolled at the Academy of Fine Art there at seventeen and studied landscape painting and drawing. His uncle Antonio Pasini, a painter and manuscript illuminator, helped him early on. By 1852 he had shown thirty designs of castles, made into lithographs. He is best known for Orientalist subjects. His style was late Romantic.

Zoffany came from a noble Hungarian and Bohemian family, and his father was a cabinet maker and court architect. He began in a sculptor's workshop in Ellwangen and went on to study in Regensburg. He worked mainly in England, and also in Italy and India. His paintings hang in the National Gallery, the Tate and the Royal Collection, and in India, the United States and Australia. He was born Johannes Josephus Zaufallij and died in 1810.

Joseph Nash was the oldest son of a reverend who owned Manor House School in Croydon. He studied with Augustus Charles Pugin and travelled with him to France to prepare architectural drawings for Paris and its Environs. His major work was the four-volume Mansions of England in the Olden Time, published from 1839. He became an associate of the Society of Painters in Water Colours in 1834.

Stockholm is where Georg Engelhard Schröder first saw daylight, the son of a goldsmith from Nuremberg who had emigrated there. He studied under David von Krafft until 1703. Then he spent twenty-one years travelling most of Europe. After northern Germany he went to Italy, staying five years in Venice, copying old masters and painting views of the city. There he met the pastellist Rosalba Carriera. In Rome he was inspired by Baroque artists such as Carlo Dolci.

Jan Baptist Weenix could not speak well, apparently from a medical condition, and he loved reading, so his mother sent him to work for a bookseller. The bookseller could not manage him. He drew whenever he could, according to his son Jan. Weenix grew up near Amsterdam's harbor, the son of an architect. He mainly brought the Italian harbor scene into Dutch art. Late in life he painted large still lifes of dead game or dogs.

Tani Bunchō's father was the poet Tani Rokkoku, and the family served the Tayasu house, so Bunchō inherited samurai status and a stipend. In his youth he studied Kanō school technique under Katō Bunrei. After Bunrei died he worked with masters of other schools, including the literati painter Kitayama Kangen, and built a wide range of styles, Chinese, Japanese and European. He rose to prominence as a retainer of Matsudaira Sadanobu. He also wrote poetry.

At eleven Carlo Dolci attempted a whole figure of Saint John and a head of the infant Christ, and they got some approval. He was apprenticed young to Jacopo Vignali in Florence. He was not prolific. His biographer Baldinucci said he would take weeks over a single foot. That painstaking technique made him unsuited to large frescoes. He painted chiefly sacred subjects, mostly small, with a few life-size pictures, and often repeated them in many versions.

Emil Carlsen grew up in Copenhagen in an artistic family. His mother painted, and a cousin who influenced him later directed a school. He emigrated from Denmark to the United States and became known for still lifes. Later he added landscapes and seascapes. He was elected to the National Academy of Design. For more than forty years he taught in Chicago, San Francisco and New York.

Francesco Trevisani's masterpiece is the set of frescoes in San Silvestro in Capite, painted in 1695 and 1696 under strong influence from Carlo Maratta. He was born in Capodistria, today Koper in Slovenia, where his father, an architect, taught him the first rudiments of design. He studied in Venice under Antonio Zanchi and then Joseph Heintz the Younger. Around 1678 he moved to Rome. No paintings survive from his early Venetian period.

From an early age Erik Pauelsen had his mind set on becoming an artist. He went to Copenhagen and studied at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts, where he won the large gold medal and the travel scholarship in 1777. He travelled to Rome by way of Hamburg, Düsseldorf and Paris. He is most notable for landscapes and was also a popular portraitist. He never matched the success of his contemporaries Jens Juel and Nicolai Abildgaard. He died in 1790.

Francesco Botticini's father painted playing cards, the trade from which he probably got his first training. By 1459 he was a salaried assistant in the workshop of Neri di Bicci in Florence. He left it in 1460. Few of his works are documented, but a large body of altarpieces, dozens of small religious panels and a few portraits are confidently attributed to him on style. He stayed in Florence until he died in 1498.

Houbraken confused Karel van Mander III with his father, the Younger, but says he learned from him and became a good portrait painter. A portrait of Christian IV got a poem from Joost van den Vondel, and so did one of Vondel himself with grey hair. According to the RKD he was influenced by Frans Hals. He worked in Copenhagen in 1631 and went to Italy from 1635 to 1638. He settled in Copenhagen afterwards.

Tribute to Caesar, Louis Gallait's first picture, won a prize at the Salon of Ghent in 1832. He had first studied in Tournai under Philippe Auguste Hennequin, then went to Antwerp to study under Mathieu Ignace van Brée. The large painting of the abdication of Charles V built his reputation. His works were esteemed for realism, faithful costumes and color. He lay at the basis of a revival of history painting in Belgium and was a distinguished portrait painter.

Johann Heinrich Schönfeld was blind in his left eye from birth and could use his right hand only for simple tasks, so he was not trained as a goldsmith like his father. He took painting lessons from Caspar Sichelbein in Memmingen instead. In 1633, at the height of the Thirty Years' War, he fled to Italy, living first in Rome and then in Naples. He went home in 1651 and married a year later. He and his wife had eight children.

Chen Hongshou once trained under Lan Ying and was skilled at painting peculiar human figures, as well as landscapes and flowers and birds. He used plump, deep brushwork and precise color, which gave him a style of his own. He often made book illustrations and portraits for weaving. His two masterpieces, Shui Hu Ye Zi and Bo Gu Ye Zi, are rare examples of their kind from the Ming and Qing periods. He lived from 1598 to 1652.

His brothers were Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, but Ludwig Emil Grimm became a painter and etcher. He studied in Kassel and then at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich. In 1814 he served as an officer in the campaign against Napoleon. Two years later he went to Italy, where Carl Ernst Christoph Hess taught him engraving, and he published his first work, a sketchbook of engravings from the trip. He drew the frontispiece for a later edition of the fairy tales.

Rich patrons all over Europe wanted portraits by Jacopo Amigoni, who began in Venice. He turned out to be born in Naples, despite older claims for Venice. At first he painted mythological and religious scenes. As his patrons spread northward, he made many parlour pictures of gods in sensuous languor or at games. His style influenced Giuseppe Nogari, and Antonio Zucchi was among his pupils. From 1717 he is documented in Bavaria.

Anders Askevold was the second oldest of ten siblings, and his father was a teacher and member of parliament. At thirteen he began training in Bergen under the landscape painter Hans Leganger Reuch. In 1855 he went to Düsseldorf and stayed three years, training under Hans Gude. He continued in Paris and Munich. Fjord landscapes of western Norway, in a romantic national style, are what he is best known for.

Walter Wilcox explored the Canadian Rockies around Lake Louise in the 1890s and discovered Paradise Valley and Desolation Valley, and Prospector Valley too. He made the first ascent of Mount Temple on 17 August 1894, with Samuel Allen and Lewis Frissell. He also made the first ascents of Mount Aberdeen and Cheops Mountain. J. Norman Collie named Mount Wilcox in the Columbia Icefield area after him in 1898. He went to Phillips Academy and then Yale.

Hans Holbein the Elder came from a celebrated family of painters in Augsburg. His father was Michael Holbein and his brother Sigmund. His name appears in the Augsburg tax books in 1494, replacing his father's. He died in Issenheim, in Alsace. Both his sons became artists and printmakers: Ambrosius, and Hans the Younger, who both had their first painting lessons from him. The exact date of his own birth is unknown.

Little written evidence remains of Hans Springinklee's life. He was born in Nuremberg in the early 1490s. A chronicler wrote later that he had lived with Albrecht Dürer and learned his craft from him. His first woodcuts date from 1512 or 1513, and in 1520 the council of Nuremberg commissioned him to decorate rooms in the castle before a visit. He probably left the city soon after. He died no later than 1540.

James Nairn studied at the Glasgow School of Art for four years from 1879 and then enrolled at the Académie Julian in Paris. In the 1880s he showed at the Glasgow Institute and the Royal Scottish Academy and had links with the Glasgow Boys. He moved from Glasgow to Dunedin for his health in 1890. A year later he took a job as art instructor at the Wellington Technical School. He believed in painting outdoors, and he strongly influenced New Zealand painting.

Georg Emanuel Opiz also wrote now-forgotten historical novels under the pseudonym Bohemus. He grew up in Prague, where his father was a tax official, writer and magazine editor who corresponded with Casanova. His brother was the botanist Philipp Maximilian Opiz. Georg took a law degree while studying drawing and painting in his spare time, and in 1793 he went on to the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts. He worked as a painter and graphic artist. He died in 1841.

Jan van de Velde the younger was the son of the calligrapher Jan van de Velde the Elder, and himself the father of a still life painter. He was apprenticed to the engraver Jacob Matham in 1613 and joined the Haarlem guild a year later. After that he probably visited Italy. He is better known for his etching and engraving than for painting. His subjects were mostly animals, landscapes and still lifes. He died in 1641.

Julien Dupré was expected to join the family jewelry business, and he began working in a lace shop. Then the war of 1870 and the siege of Paris forced his parents to close their shop. With time on his hands he took evening courses at the École des Arts Décoratifs, and that led him into the École des Beaux-Arts. There he studied with Isidore Pils and Henri Lehmann. In the mid-1870s he travelled to Picardy.

Benjamin Robert Haydon painted grand historical pictures on an enormous scale, and that scale hurt his commercial success. So did his tactless dealings with patrons. Money trouble followed him all his life and several times landed him in prison for debt. He was the only son of a prosperous printer and publisher in Plymouth. He also painted a few contemporary subjects and portraits. He died in 1846.

Jean-François Brémond, a pupil of Ingres and Couder, was born in Paris in 1807. He produced portraits as well as historical pictures. Among his paintings are a Portrait of his Daughter, Saint Francis of Assisi, Saint Catharine of Alexandria, The Entry of Christ into Jerusalem and Susannah in the Bath. He died in Paris in 1868. Bryan's Dictionary of 1886 lists him in its entry.

His parents wanted François-Auguste Biard in the clergy, but he spent his time learning to paint, starting at a wallpaper factory in Lyon. He later attended the École des Beaux-Arts, where he worked with Pierre Révoil and then Fleury François Richard. His studies were sporadic and much was self-taught. He travelled to Italy, Greece and the Middle East, and he is known for adventurous journeys and paintings of what he saw, such as The Slave Trade.

Rural winter snow scenes made George Henry Durrie popular, especially after Currier and Ives reproduced them as lithographs. He was one of six children in a New Haven family. His father was a partner in the printing firm of Durrie and Peck, stationers and publishers. In 1837 his father contracted with the engraver and portrait painter Nathaniel Jocelyn to teach George and his brother John. He died in 1863.

Matthijs Naiveu worked as the hop inspector for the brewers of Amsterdam, and according to Houbraken he was still alive and painting there. He learned drawing from Abraham Toorenvliet and painting from Gerrit Dou. His genre pieces show merry company interiors with people drinking tea or playing cards, and also visits to newborn babies. His largest work was a Seven Works of Mercy, which Houbraken found his best. He was born in Leiden in 1647.

Charles Robert Leslie painted a portrait of the actor George Frederick Cooke from memory of seeing him on stage in Philadelphia, and it looked so promising that a fund was raised to send the young artist to Europe. His parents were American, but he was born in London and returned there to spend his career. He had been apprenticed to a bookseller as a youth. He left for London in 1811 and wrote as well as painted.

Otto Marseus van Schrieck was called snuffelaer, the ferreter, and he is best known for pictures of forest flora and fauna. He was born in Nijmegen and spent the years 1652 to 1657 in Rome and Florence with Matthias Withoos and Willem van Aelst. There he joined the Bentvueghels. Later he worked at the court of the Grand Duke of Tuscany, travelled in England and France, and settled in Amsterdam. He married the daughter of an engraver in 1664.

The son of a baker, Pieter Thijs had three masters. He trained as a cabinet painter with Artus Deurwerdeers, in the style of Frans Francken the Younger's workshop. Later he moved to the circle of Anthony van Dyck. His style was close to Van Dyck's courtly elegance. He worked in Antwerp and was very successful, painting for courts in Brussels and The Hague and for many religious institutions. He painted portraits, religious works and history paintings.

August Leu travelled in Norway in 1843 and 1847, and his large Norwegian pictures raised awareness in Germany of that country's scenery. He had studied with Johann Wilhelm Schirmer, a landscape painter of the Düsseldorf school. Later he travelled widely in the Alps. He lived for a time in Brussels and returned to Düsseldorf. In 1882 he moved to Berlin, where he became a royal professor and a member of the Academy of Art.

He is often called Franz Steinfeld the Younger because his father, also Franz, was a sculptor. The son first studied sculpting with him, but the engraver Francesco Vasanova suggested the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna instead. There he studied with Laurenz Janscha, Martin von Molitor and Albert Christoph Dies. A study trip to the Rhineland and the Netherlands in 1805 drew him to the works of Jacob van Ruisdael. He painted landscapes. He married in 1815.

Antoni Piotrowski grew up in a family of sheet iron workers near Kunów in Russian-ruled Poland. From 1869 he studied painting with Wojciech Gerson in Warsaw. Then he went to Munich, where he studied with Wilhelm Lindenschmit the Younger, and in Kraków with Jan Matejko. During the Liberation of Bulgaria he worked as a war correspondent and illustrator for Western European weeklies. He painted in Romanticist and realist styles. He lived from 1853 to 1924.

Ernest Hébert moved from Grenoble to Paris in 1835 to study law, the profession of his father the notary. At the same time he took lessons in the workshops of the sculptor David d'Angers and the history painter Paul Delaroche, though he was mostly self-taught. At 22 he succeeded at the Salon with a painting of a prison scene. In 1839 the Académie des Beaux-Arts awarded him the Prix de Rome for a biblical composition.

Pedro Orrente's father, a merchant from Marseille, had settled in Murcia in 1573. A painter named Juan de Arizmendi, a friend, probably gave Pedro his first lessons. By 1600 Pedro was in Toledo, hired to make an altarpiece in the village of Guadarrama, which has not survived. He became one of the first artists in that part of Spain to paint in a Naturalistic style. Early Baroque is his period.

Franciabigio's real name may have been Francesco di Cristofano. He worked under Albertinelli until about 1506. In 1505 he befriended Andrea del Sarto, and soon the two set up a shared shop in the Piazza del Grano. He paid close attention to anatomy and perspective, though his figures are often squat. Vasari claimed that he surpassed all his contemporaries in fresco. He died in 1525.

Card and backgammon players, brothel scenes, dancing and music making in elegant rooms, inns and gardens were Christoffel van der Laemen's favorite themes. He specialized in merry company scenes with elegant figures. His father was a painter and art dealer from Antwerp who worked in Brussels, and for that reason Brussels is proposed as his birthplace. Nobody knows for certain whether it was Brussels or Antwerp. He died around 1651.

Little is known about the early life of Jean Clouet. Art historians assume he came from the Burgundian Netherlands, though his known work was done in France. He became court painter to King Francis I. With his son François he counts among the leading portrait painters working in France in the 16th century. The two are best known for accomplished drawings in black chalk and red chalk. He died in 1540 or 1541.

Solomon Joseph Solomon helped develop camouflage in the First World War, working on tree observation posts and arguing tirelessly for camouflage netting. He studied in turn at the Heatherley School, the Royal Academy Schools, the Munich Academy and the École des Beaux-Arts, under Alexandre Cabanel. His sister Lily Delissa Joseph was a painter too. He was a founding member of the New English Art Club and later a member of the Royal Academy.

Two of Fujishima Takeji's older brothers died of injuries from the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877, and he became head of the household while still in his early teens. He came from an ex-samurai family in Kagoshima, and his family had a long link to the Satsuma domain. He developed Romanticism and impressionism within yōga, the Western-style painting movement in Japan. In his later years the Art Nouveau movement influenced him.

Samuel Cousins was the interpreter of Sir Thomas Lawrence in mezzotint. Born in Exeter, he was apprenticed to Samuel William Reynolds, for whom he engraved many of the little mezzotints in a set of three hundred and sixty. He became a full member of the Royal Academy in 1855 and gave it £15,000 in trust to pay annuities to elderly artists. He died unmarried in London and is buried in Highgate Cemetery.

Details of Cornelis van Dalem's life are scarce. He was likely born in Antwerp, and his father was a nobleman from Tholen who worked there as a cloth merchant and took part in the local chamber of rhetoric. Van Dalem was a Flemish painter and draughtsman. He drew on his humanistic education to bring new themes into landscape painting, and he looked for new ways of showing them. That made him an important contributor to landscape art in the Low Countries.

A painting called Cotton got Kindred McLeary into trouble in 1928. He had entered it in a national show at the Witte Memorial Museum in San Antonio. It showed an African-American woman reclining in a cotton field with several men around her, one of them strumming a guitar. Some artists and ministers attacked it as obscene, but the museum's curator defended it. McLeary studied architecture at the University of Texas and taught there.

Charley Toorop was the daughter of the painter Jan Toorop. She married the philosopher Henk Fernhout in 1912 and later divorced him. Her son Edgar became a painter, and her other son John became a filmmaker who often worked with Joris Ivens. Her daughter-in-law was the photographer Eva Besnyö. Toorop herself painted and made lithographs. She lived from 1891 to 1955.

In the 1820s Giovanni Boggi was at his artistic peak, an engraver and painter. Several of his works are on display at the Bibliothèque Nationale in Paris. He was noted especially for portraits of important Greeks from the War of Greek Independence, including Markos Botsaris and Theodoros Kolokotronis. He also made portraits of Francesco Algarotti and Luigi Lanzi. He died in 1832.

Claude Lorrain came from the Duchy of Lorraine but spent most of his life in Italy. He painted landscapes at a time when few western artists did, outside the Dutch. To lift them toward history painting he added a few small figures, usually from the Bible or classical mythology. By the end of the 1630s he was the leading landscapist in Italy and earned large fees. His landscapes gradually grew larger. He died in 1682.

Jean-Joseph-Xavier Bidauld first studied painting with his elder brother in Lyons. In 1783 he went to Paris, where an art dealer and perfume seller named Dulac paid for his travels in Italy. He lived five years in Rome. In 1791 he entered the Salon for the first time and took part regularly afterwards. In 1792 he began to get official commissions. In 1823 he became the first landscape painter elected to the Académie des Beaux-Arts.

Liévin De Winne painted the official portrait of Leopold I on which Belgium's first postage stamp was based. He studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts of Ghent. A government grant in 1850 let him travel to Paris, where he shared a studio with Jules Breton, who later wrote his biography. From 1861 he lived in Belgium again as a portrait painter to high society. His direct style broke decisively with earlier romantic portraiture.
Chester Harding painted portraits of prominent figures in the United States and England. He was born in 1792 and died in 1866.

Jean LeClerc studied with the Venetian master Carlo Saraceni. He was born and died in Nancy, in the Duchy of Lorraine. His style was Baroque, more specifically tenebrist, and he is known for mastery of nocturnal light effects and the luminosity of his scenes. Only six authenticated paintings remain, but many etchings and engravings have survived. He was buried in 1633.
